CASE PUD 2026-000031 ENTRY NO. 107 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 08/21/2026 - PAGE 1 OF 9




           BEFORE THE CORPORATION COMMISSION OF THE STATE OF OKLAHOMA

          IN THE MATTER OF THE APPLICATION OF                     )
          OKLAHOMA GAS AND ELECTRIC COMPANY                       ) Case No. PUD2026-000031
          FOR COMMISSION APPROVAL OF ELECTRIC                     )
          SERVICE AGREEMENTS AND PREAPPROVAL                      )
          OF CAPACITY PURCHASE AGREEMENTS                         )
          PURSUANT TO 17 O.S. § 286(C)                            )




                                             Rebuttal Testimony

                                                       of

                                            Jason J. Thenmadathil

                                                 on behalf of

                                     Oklahoma Gas and Electric Company




                                               August 21, 2026




         Rebuttal Testimony of Jason J. Thenmadathil                                   Page 1 of 8
         Case No. PUD2026-000031
 CASE PUD 2026-000031 ENTRY NO. 107 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 08/21/2026 - PAGE 2 OF 9




                                                 Jason J. Thenmadathil
                                                  Rebuttal Testimony

    1    Q.     Please state your name and business address.
    2    A.     My name is Jason J. Thenmadathil. My business address is 321 North Harvey, Oklahoma
    3           City, Oklahoma 73102.
    4
    5    Q.     Are you the same Jason J. Thenmadathil who filed Direct Testimony in this case on
    6           May 1, 2026?
    7    A.     Yes, I am.
    8
    9    Q.     What is the purpose of your testimony?
   10    A.     The purpose of my testimony is to respond to arguments raised in the Responsive
   11           Testimony of the Attorney General (“AG”), Oklahoma Sustainability Network (“OSN”),
   12           and the Public Utility Division (“PUD”).
   13
   14    Q.     Have intervenors criticized the Company’s analysis on the grounds that it only
   15           examines the benefits associated with allocating existing system costs over a larger
   16           billing determinant base?
   17    A.     Yes. Intervenors contend that the analysis in my Direct Testimony reflects only one side
   18           of the equation because it does not attempt to quantify future generation additions or other
   19           potential costs that may ultimately result from serving the data center load.1
   20
   21    Q.     What is your response to that concern?
   22    A.     Our analysis was intentionally structured to evaluate only those impacts that are currently
   23           known and measurable at the time this analysis was performed. I explicitly stated in my
   24           Direct Testimony that the analysis was limited to the downward rate pressure resulting
   25           from spreading existing utility costs across additional load.2       The analysis was not
   26           presented as a comprehensive forecast of all possible future costs and benefits associated
   27           with the data center over the life of the contract.


         1
                Beling Responsive, 22:1–23:13, Givens Responsive 13:4–14.
         2
                Thenmadathil Direct, 5:1–9.

         Rebuttal Testimony of Jason J. Thenmadathil                                             Page 2 of 8
         Case No. PUD2026-000031
 CASE PUD 2026-000031 ENTRY NO. 107 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 08/21/2026 - PAGE 3 OF 9




    1    Q.     Why did you not include estimates of future generation resources or other potential
    2           system investments?
    3    A.     Such estimates are not known and measurable at this time. Currently, the Company has
    4           not presented future generation facilities, the timing of such facilities, and the costs to the
    5           Commission for pre-approval. Any attempt to quantify such impacts would rely on
    6           assumptions regarding unknown future events. As a result, any estimate would be highly
    7           speculative and would not provide the same level of reliability as the known and
    8           measurable rate case cost of service and contract demand data utilized in my analysis.
    9
   10    Q.     How do you respond to the argument that future costs should be weighed against the
   11           benefits you identified?
   12    A.     The future is a two-way street.       Future costs are only one side of the uncertainty
   13           surrounding future system conditions. If one assumes that future unknown costs should be
   14           considered, then it is equally important to recognize that future unknown benefits also exist.
   15           For example, future transmission investment, distribution investment, generation
   16           resources, software investment, and other system costs incurred for the benefit of all
   17           customers may be spread across a larger load base due to the addition of the data center.
   18           Those future cost sharing benefits are not reflected in my analysis for the same reason
   19           future generation costs are not reflected: neither can be reliably quantified today.
   20
   21    Q.     Do the Electric Service Agreements (“ESAs”)contain provisions to address concerns
   22           regarding possible future adverse impacts resulting from the future costs needed to
   23           serve Google?
   24    A.     Yes, the ESAs contain a protective provision requiring the Company to study and present
   25           the impacts of serving the data center load in future rate proceedings, including whether
   26           the customer’s service by OG&E is resulting in adverse impacts to other customers. This
   27           provision serves as an important safeguard. Rather than attempting to forecast uncertain
   28           outcomes today, the provision requires the Company to use actual experience and actual
   29           cost data for the Commission to review.




         Rebuttal Testimony of Jason J. Thenmadathil                                               Page 3 of 8
         Case No. PUD2026-000031
 CASE PUD 2026-000031 ENTRY NO. 107 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 08/21/2026 - PAGE 4 OF 9




    1    Q.     Why is that approach preferable?
    2    A.     It is preferable because it allows decisions to be made using actual data rather than
    3           assumptions. If future costs exceed benefits and create adverse rate impacts to other
    4           customers, those impacts can be identified and addressed in a future rate proceeding. In
    5           other words, the ESAs recognize that forecasts are inherently uncertain and therefore
    6           establishes a mechanism for evaluating actual outcomes once they are known.
    7
    8    Q.     Please address the general recommendations of the parties regarding the “fail safe”
    9           adverse impact analysis included in the contract.
   10    A.     All the parties generally agreed to the concept of the adverse impact analysis. The AG
   11           agreed with the concept but had recommendations on how to specifically conduct the
   12           analysis.
   13
   14    Q.     What is the Company’s recommendation regarding the specific parameters of the
   15           study?
   16    A.     Although parties have raised some proposals for how the study should be calculated,
   17           OG&E would not recommend the Commission adopt specific parameters surrounding the
   18           study at this time, until actual known and measurable data is available to conduct the study.
   19           The Company will provide the full “with and without” study in a general rate filing which
   20           includes Google as a customer and provide all workpapers and results along with testimony
   21           explaining how the study was conducted. All parties will have the opportunity to review
   22           the study at that time and make recommendations to the Commission regarding the
   23           methodology of the study based on the actual data.
   24
   25    Q.     AG witness Beling recommends that allocation factors should be updated more
   26           frequently, and that there be a true-up for Construction Work in Progress
   27           (“CWIP”).3 How do you respond to these recommendations?
   28    A.     In Case No. PUD2025-000082, OG&E proposed a true-up mechanism and annual
   29           allocation update for its requested CWIP rider. Although that tariff was not approved,
   30           OG&E intends to recommend a similar mechanism in the event it requests CWIP in the

         3
                Id. at 29:3–15.

         Rebuttal Testimony of Jason J. Thenmadathil                                             Page 4 of 8
         Case No. PUD2026-000031
 CASE PUD 2026-000031 ENTRY NO. 107 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 08/21/2026 - PAGE 5 OF 9




    1           future. I would also note that AG witness Beling’s arguments about regulatory lag of
    2           allocation factors are compelling reasons why the Commission should consider adopting
    3           some sort of performance-based rate mechanism. Such a mechanism could true up costs
    4           and allocation factors every year.
    5
    6    Q.     AG witness Mr. Beling and OIEC witness Mr. Garrett argue that any future
    7           transmission costs associated with the Google load should be directly borne by
    8           Google.4 How would the Company approach analyzing transmission costs?
    9    A.     The treatment of any future transmission costs associated with Google should be addressed
   10           in a future proceeding, such as the large load tariff case or a general rate case. In a future
   11           rate case, costs will be known and a full cost of service study can be performed, along with
   12           the adverse impact study. Regardless, allocation impacts resulting from Google and other
   13           large load customers are a fair issue to raise and should be addressed in future proceedings.
   14           In addition, it is also important to understand that with the “fail safe” mechanism mentioned
   15           in the contract, customers would not be adversely affected from additional transmission
   16           costs needed specifically for Google in the “with and without” study.
   17
   18    Q.     Please address the PUD’s recommendation regarding the timing of performing the
   19           adverse impact analysis for fuel and base rates.5
   20    A.     While I appreciate the PUD’s objective of regularly monitoring potential customer impacts,
   21           I believe the Company’s proposed approach of performing the adverse impact analysis in
   22           an annual fuel prudency review or a general rate case is more appropriate. The purpose of
   23           the “with and without” analysis is to determine whether the data center has resulted in
   24           adverse impacts to other customers by considering both the costs associated with serving
   25           the data center and the allocation benefits associated with spreading system costs over
   26           additional load. A general rate case is the proceeding in which the Company's revenue
   27           requirement, cost allocation methodologies, and billing determinants are updated and used
   28           to establish customer rates. Accordingly, performing the analysis in that context allows
   29           the Commission to evaluate both the costs and benefits of the data center using the same


         4
                Beling Responsive, 28:7–17; Garrett Responsive 14:3–12.
         5
                Givens Responsive, 19:21–20:5.

         Rebuttal Testimony of Jason J. Thenmadathil                                              Page 5 of 8
         Case No. PUD2026-000031
 CASE PUD 2026-000031 ENTRY NO. 107 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 08/21/2026 - PAGE 6 OF 9




    1           data and assumptions that support the rates ultimately approved for customers. To the
    2           extent the PUD proposes tracking annual impacts, that approach would be more appropriate
    3           alongside a performance-based rate plan, where rates are updated annually and financial
    4           and allocation impacts can be studied.
    5
    6    Q.     Do you believe more frequent reviews may be appropriate for fuel-related impacts?
    7    A.     Yes. Fuel costs are already subject to periodic review outside of base rate proceedings and
    8           are adjusted through existing, separate regulatory mechanisms. For that reason, the
    9           Company believes the fuel-related impacts associated with the data center should be
   10           evaluated on an annual basis through these proceedings. OG&E believes these reviews
   11           should be evaluated through a Commission proceeding, where all parties have an
   12           opportunity to review and make recommendations to the Commission. The appropriate
   13           methodology can be determined in a future rate case or other Commission proceeding. For
   14           purposes of evaluating base-rate impacts, I believe a general rate case remains the most
   15           appropriate forum because it provides a complete and contemporaneous review of both the
   16           costs and allocation benefits associated with serving the data center.
   17
   18    Q.     Please summarize your testimony.
   19    A.     The analysis presented in my Direct Testimony focused on known and measurable impacts.
   20           Future costs and future benefits are both unknown today and OG&E has appropriately
   21           proposed a “with and without” evaluation in a general rate using actual costs and benefits
   22           for the Commission to evaluate. In addition, the ESAs appropriately address uncertainty
   23           through a “fail safe” provision requiring future evaluation of actual system impacts and
   24           providing a forum for any adverse effects to be identified and addressed using real data.
   25
   26    Q.     Does your testimony address all issues raised by parties in their Responsive
   27           Testimony?
   28    A.     No. My Rebuttal Testimony is limited in scope and does not address all issues raised in
   29           this proceeding. My silence on any issue should not be construed as agreement with
   30           another party’s testimony.
